effective implementation of the scheme.  Transparency in selection of the Yuva Sathees must also be ensured.  The main
criteria for selection may be the social commitment of the candidates.  The Committee expresses its doubt about the
efficacy of 10-20 Sathees in a district as well as adequacy of Rs. 1000/- per month honorarium for them. 
 
8.4   The Committee notes that this scheme has taken the place of erstwhile National Reconstruction Corps Scheme,
which continued upto March, 2003.   It has taken two years in formulation of the revised scheme.   The Committee hopes
that this scheme would not suffer from the shortcomings experienced in the implementation of the earlier scheme.

country are yet to be opened or fully operationalised. The Ministry should take up the matter with the State Governments
for removal of bottlenecks in setting up/operationalising of these sub-centres without any further delay.  The SAI
centres/sub-centres should be opened preferably in those States, which have shown commendable performance in the
national as well as international events.
 
17.9     The Committee notes that 25 Navodaya Vidyalayas have been identified to be supported by the Ministry under

scheme under which lot of support is provided for creating infrastructure for training etc. of the budding sportspersons.

to the regular studies; sports may not be priority for them.  Secondly, these schools being purely residential, students
from other neighboring schools may not be able to use the facilities provided there.  The Committee feels, emphasis of
the Ministry while opening the NST Centres, should be to the normal schools particularly in the rural areas where the
infrastructure could be used in a better way.   
 
XVIII   COMMONWEALTH GAMES, 2010
18.1     A provision of Rs. 45.50 crores has been projected for Commonwealth Games, 2010 for the year 2005-06, in the
overall budget of Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, as against the Ministry's projection of Rs. 115.00 crores.           
The provision has been made to meet expenditure on up-gradation of SAI infrastructure; requirements of funds for
construction/ functioning of Apex Committee, Sub-committee of GOM and the organising committee; requirement of
funds for the Games Village; and expenditure on study and assessment tours in connection with conceptualization and
assessment of the infrastructure.
 
18.2     The Committee notes that a task force has been set up in the Ministry with representatives from CPWD and SAI.
CPWD has been assigned the consultancy to undertake the work of condition survey and special inspection of all five
stadia in Delhi and to prepare a detailed report alongwith the estimated expenditure for altering, enhancing and retrofitting
the existing stadia. The final report is expected to be received in August, 2005.
 
18.3     The Committee hopes that the report of Task Force would be submitted in time so that the action in this regard is
initiated timely. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should be provided adequate fund at RE stage so that the
works pertaining to Commonwealth Games, 2010 were not delayed. A plan should be chalked for phase-wise
development of the infrastructure and the money be spent judiciously. The Committee feels that efforts should be made
to build proper infrastructure in time-bound manner with a view to avoiding last minute pressure of work.
 
            While creating infrastructure for the Commonwealth Games, we should not ignore preparation/training of our
sportspersons. This should be treated as an opportunity to enhance our nation's prestige by winning more and more
medals. Selection and training of prospective participants must take place now so that they get enough time to prepare
themselves.
 
18.4     The Committee feels that hosting 2010 Commonwealth Games is a privilege accompanied with a lot of

IV.       BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
 
The Committee feels that the Ministry's projection for the annual plan, 2005-06 was quite justified because it
constituted only 10% increase over the previous year’s allocations and also because the Ministry has to fulfill its
obligation for the preparations of the Commonwealth Games, 2010 and expansion of NSS upto the school level.  There
appears to be no justification in applying cut to its allocations, particularly when the Ministry was
able to spend more than 66.72% of its allocation upto December, 2004, as per the existing norms in
this regard.  (Para 4.1)
 
The Committee considers it disappointingly low in view of the mandate of the Ministry being to develop the
personality of our youth as also involving them in nation-building activities.  This group, which constitutes nearly 40 per
cent of total population of India, is the most vibrant and potent segment of our society.  Allocation below one per cent to
youth development and sports reflects a low preference.  The Committee is of the considered opinion that there is a
strong case for adequate allocation for the Ministry in the coming years.  Department's demand for a share in the funds
collected through education cess must be considered favourably, particularly for expansion of NSS upto 9 th class and
also in all the remaining schools. (Para 4.2)
 
Committee’s attention has also been drawn by the disturbing trend of under-utilisation of funds meant for NE
States both under the Youth and Sports Programmes during the Tenth Plan period so far.   The Committee is also
disturbed by the status of scheme of ‘Promotion of Sports Among Disabled.’   Not even single rupee could be spent
under this scheme against the Ninth Plan allocation of  Rs. 15 lakhs .  Position remains unchanged during the Tenth Plan
also so far.   This Scheme has been continuing on paper only.  Performance Budget of the Department for 2005-06
indicates that the Scheme is now being merged with the Scheme relating to Events.   The Committee does not appreciate
the way scheme  ‘Promotion of Sports among Disabled’, which is meant to serve the under-privileged class of society, is
being handled.  It needs to be strengthened. (Para 4.3)
 
            Even during the Ninth Plan, funds remained underutilised in different categories.  For example, of the total Ninth
Plan outlay of Rs. 352.24 crores for Youth Welfare, only Rs. 336.94 crores could be spent.  The schemes suffering most
were:  National Reconstruction Corps, Youth Hostels and Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Youth Development.  Similarly,
spending Rs. 558.50 crores in Ninth Plan period against an outlay of Rs. 472.61 under Sports and Physical Education
also indicates towards fiscal (mal)practices such as unspent balances or re-appropriation etc.  The Committee is of the
view that these situations - under-utilization as well as unspent balances - indicate that both our delivery mechanism as
well as system of flow of funds are not foolproof and need to be streamlined further.  It reflects a poor physical
performance because it is directly related to the financial performance. (Para 4.4)
 
            While appreciating the formulation of quarterly Action Plans during Tenth Plan by the Ministry, the Committee
feels that it has not been able to achieve the desired results. The Committee would like to emphasize the need for the
judicious and optimum utilisation of funds by the Ministry allocated for various schemes by the Ministry. (Para 4.5)
 
            The Committee is of the view that a detailed review of the schemes showing poor performance should be
undertaken so as to identify the shortcomings and initiate remedial measures. The Ministry should involve the Planning
Commission, the State Governments and other implementing agencies in this exercise. (Para 4.6)
 
            The Committee is aware of the structural problems inherent in our system from Union level down to the
Panchayats in implementing the central sector as well as centrally-sponsored schemes.  Ours being basically a
cooperative federation, States have got to play a more pro-active and coordinated role in this exercise for obtaining the
desired impact of the schemes at the ground level. (Para 4.7)

REPORT
           
The Manipur University Bill 2005 seeks to convert the existing Manipur University into a Central University with
a view to ensure its accelerated development and minimize the imbalance in educational facilities in the North Eastern
Region.
 
2.         The Manipur University was established at Imphal in June 1980, under the Manipur University Act, 1980 enacted
by the Manipur Legislative Assembly.  Prior to the establishment of this University, the Centre of Post Graduate Studies
of the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), established at Imphal in the year 1972, was catering to the educational needs
of the students of Manipur at the postgraduate level and the undergraduate colleges, including some professional
colleges, in the State were affiliated to Guwahati University.
 
3.         The Committee was informed that with the coming into force of the Manipur University Act, 1980, Guwahati
University ceased to exercise jurisdiction in the State of Manipur and the erstwhile Centre of Post Graduate Studies of
JNU was merged with the newly established Manipur University.
 
4.         The Committee was further informed that the Manipur University has at present 23 post-graduate teaching
departments under three Schools of Studies.  It also has 73 affiliated colleges including a medical college, three law
colleges, six teacher-training colleges, three technical/engineering colleges and a college of physical education and
sports.  The number of students presently enrolled in the teaching departments and affiliated colleges of the University is
about 2,000 and 30,000 respectively.
 
5.         According to the Department of Secondary and Higher Education, as the Manipur University started without any
foundation grant and could not get adequate plan assistance from the Government in the succeeding years, it has not been
in a position to create the required infrastructure and to diversify its courses  to the  extent required  so far.  It is
surrounded by central universities of the North-Eastern Region at Kohima, Silchar, Tezpur, Aizawl and Shillong.  This
has caused a huge imbalance in educational facilities within the region, and a consequent migration of teachers, students
and researchers in search of better infrastructural and academic facilities in other states.  Not only this, many years of
insurgency in different parts of the State resulted in the exodus of a large number of students from the State to places like
Delhi.

164threport of committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/164threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:36]
 
6.         Against this backdrop and the fact that the State Government, with its limited resources, was not in a position to
provide adequate funding for the development of the Manipur University, there had been a persistent demand for making
it as a central university.  Besides repeated requests from the State Government, the Manipur Legislative Assembly had
also passed unanimous resolutions to this effect on the 9th July, 1999 and more recently on the 13th March, 2003.
 
7.         Accordingly, the Manipur University Bill 2005, has been introduced in the Rajya Sabha for the establishment and
incorporation of Manipur University as a central university and for repealing of the existing Manipur University Act,
1980, enacted by the Manipur Legislative Assembly.  The Bill is broadly based on the pattern of the University of
Mizoram, the most recent of the North-Eastern Universities.
 
8.         The salient features of the aforesaid Bill are as under:
(i)                  The Bill seeks to establish and incorporate the existing Manipur University, a state university of
Manipur, under the proposed Central Act by the same name of 'Manipur University' with perpetual
succession and common seal, and to provide for the matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
 
(ii)                The University would be a teaching and affiliating university with its Headquarters at Imphal and
territorial jurisdiction extending to the whole of the State of Manipur.
(iii)               It would function broadly on the pattern of the existing central universities, particularly of those of
the North-Eastern region.
(iv)              All colleges, Institutions, Schools and Departments affiliated to, or admitted to the privileges of, or
maintained by, the existing Manipur University shall stand affiliated to, or admitted to the privilege of, or
maintained by, the University.
(v)                The existing Institute of Technology, Imphal shall also be maintained by the University.
(vi)              The annual accounts of the University shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of
India and shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament along with the audit report and the annual report
of the University.
(vii)             During the transitional period, the appointment of the first Officers and the constitution of the first
Authorities of the University would be made by the Visitor for specified terms.
 
9.         The Committee, heard the Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education and took up clause-by-
clause consideration of the Bill.   It suggested the following amendments additions to various clauses of the Bill.
 
Clause 2 (m)
 
10.       The Committee notes that the definitions for `college' and `institution' provided in 2(e) and 2(m) leave some
scope for confusion, particularly in view of different categories of colleges existing/likely to exist under the Manipur
University.   For example, `constituent colleges' and 'affiliated colleges' have not been defined.   The Bill, Committee
finds, does not provide explicitly for converting an affiliated college into a constituent college. Such a demand in future,
in fact, cannot be ruled out, if a college or an institution feels that it has required standards/facilities for the purpose. 
The Committee, therefore, is of the view that there is need to amplify the definitions of the terms `constituent college',
``affiliated college' and 'institution' with a view to removing possible ambiguities in these regards.   The Committee,
therefore, recommends that necessary amendments should be brought in the relevant provision of the Bill for this
purpose. 
 
Clause 9(3)
 
11.1     Clause 9(3), page 5, provided that the Visitor shall have the right to cause an inspection to be made, by such
person or persons as he may direct, of the University, its buildings, laboratories and equipment, and of any college or
institution maintained by the University or admitted to its privileges; and also of the examinations, teaching and other
work conducted or done by the University and to cause an inquiry to be made in like manner in respect of any matter
connected with the administration or finances of the University, and the said Colleges and Institutions.

11.2     The Committee feels that libraries are important and integral constituents of the University system and need to
be included in the above provision for inspection.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in Clause 9(3) in line 33
after the word "buildings," the word 'libraries' should also be added.
 
New clause for providing Chief Rector
 
12.1     The Committee is of the view that Governors should have a role in those Central Universities which are located in
border States like Manipur. The Governor being an important link between the Centre and the State, may also be made a
part of the University, even though it is mere ceremonial.
 
12.2     The Committee, therefore, recommends that the following clause be added in the Bill after clause 9 and the entire
clauses from 10 to 46 may be renumbered accordingly:-
 
            "10.  The Governor of the State of Manipur shall be the Chief Rector of the University".
 
12.3     All the consequential changes may also be carried out in the Bill.
 
Clause 10
 
13.1     Clause 10, page 6, provides that the following shall be the officers of the University:-
(1)               the Chancellor;
(2)               the Vice-Chancellor;
(3)               the Pro-Vice Chancellor;
(4)               the Deans of Schools;
(5)               the Registrar;
(6)               the Finance Officer;
(7)               the Librarian and
(8)               such other officers as may be declared by the Statutes to be officers of the University.
 
13.2     The Committee feels that holding of examinations and awarding degrees is one of the most important functions of
a university.  If Librarian can be made as an officer, the Controller of Examinations, being an equally important
functionary of any university, should also be included as one of the officers of the university in the Act itself.  Moreover,
the post of 'Controller of Examinations' has already been provided in the existing Manipur University Act 1980, passed
by the State Legislature.
 
13.3     The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Controller of Examinations may be added as an Officer of the
University in Clause 10 of the Bill at Page 6.
 
Clause 12(3)
 
14.1     Clause 12(3), page 7, provides that the Vice-Chancellor may, if he is of the opinion that immediate action is
necessary on any matter, exercise any power conferred on any authority of the University by or under this Act and shall
report to such authority the action taken by him on such matter.
 
14.2     The Committee while accepting the rationale behind providing emergency powers to the Vice-Chancellor to deal
with urgent matters, feels that the Vice-Chancellor should be required to report such actions taken by him to the
appropriate authorities at the earliest available opportunity.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in Clause 12(3),
in line 8, the words 'at its next meeting' should be added after the word 'authority'.
 
14.3     The second proviso to clause 2(3) provides for making an 'appeal' by a person aggrieved by the emergent actions
of the VC to the EC.   The Committee feels the word 'appeal' may have different legal connotations leading sometimes to
avoidable situations.   The Committee, therefore, recommends substituting the word 'appeal' with 'representation' in line
12 of the second proviso to clause 12(3).

SCHEDULE
 
Clause 5(1) & (2) of the Statutes
 
17.1     Clause 5(1) of the Statutes provides for the appointment of Dean of a School by the Vice-Chancellor from
amongst the professors of the school for a period of three years, who shall be eligible for re-appointment.  The
Committee finds that the Statutes is silent about any criteria for selecting the professors for appointment as Dean.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the seniority as well as rotation should be included as criteria for this purpose.
           
17.2     The first proviso to clause 5 (1) of the Statutes provides that a Dean would cease to hold office at the age of 60.

the Dean is vacant or is unable to perform duties.  The Committee notes that this is a blanket power given to the Vice-

Manipur University Bill is silent about it.  The Committee is of the view that to accommodate the views of the student
community in academic as well as welfare matters, Students Council can be formed with suitable powers of
consultation.  The selection of students to the Council may be purely on the basis of merit. It, therefore, recommends that
the following may be added as Statutes at an appropriate place:
(1) There shall be constituted in the University, a Students' Council for every academic year, consisting of -
(i)                  the Dean of Students' Welfare who shall be the Chairman of the Students' Council:
(ii)                all students who have won prizes in the previous  academic year in the filed of studies, fine arts,
sports and extension work;

before the Students' Council if so permitted by the Chairman, and he shall have the right to participate in the discussions
at any meeting when the matter is taken up for consideration.
 
(2) The functions of the Students' Council shall be to make suggestions to the appropriate authorities of the
University in regard to the programmes of studies, students' welfare and other matters of importance, in regard to the
working of the University in general and such suggestions shall be made on the basis of consensus of opinion.
(3)        The Students' Council shall meet at least once in an academic year preferably in the beginning of that
year.

25.       The alumni of a university represent its proud achievements.  A regular interaction with them will help in the over
all growth of the university. The experiences and the feed back received from the past students can be an asset to the
university.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the necessary provision for an "Alumni Association" may be
incorporated in the Bill itself as has been done in the case of Mizoram  University.  The Committee recommends that the
following may be added in the statute:-

on Human Resource Development
                                                                                                      
REPORT
 
The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Bill, 2005 seeks to provide for the constitution of a National
Commission and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights and Children’s Courts for providing speedy trial of
offences against children or of violation of child rights and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The
Committee was informed that India had the largest child population in the world.  Constitution of India guarantees several
rights to the children including equality before law, free and compulsory primary education to all children between six to
fourteen years, prohibition of trafficking and forced labour by children and employment of children below the age of
fourteen years in factories, mines or hazardous occupations. The Constitution requires the State to make special
provisions for children and directs that the policy of the State shall be such that their tender age was not abused. Inspite of
Government's commitment to give children opportunities, healthy environment and facilities to develop, they continue to

165th Report of HRD Committee
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/165threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
remain vulnerable to various forms of abuse, exploitation, maltreatment, etc. 
2.         Various child-related indicators present a very dismal scenario, despite a number of child-related laws and
schemes being administered by different Departments.  The Committee was given to understand that currently child
protection, welfare and their development is being taken care of by several agencies.  As a result, many gap areas are
noticed in this regard.  The Secretary emphasised that there was a need for an authority which could take a holistic view
of the matters pertaining to children and oversee the existing programmes, policies, laws etc. for them with a view to
getting these implemented and recommend corrective measures, if required.
3.         The Government of India is a party to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) which requires
signatory States to realign their child laws with a view to make their legal, judicial and administrative systems child-
friendly as well as sensitive to interests of the child.  Thus, in view of the national as well as international developments,
the need for a National Commission for Protection of Child Rights was being felt by all those working for the
development and welfare of the children including the Government.  The Committee was informed that the draft National
Commission for Protection of Child Rights Bill, 2005 is the outcome of a prolonged and extensive interaction with all the
States/UTs, Ministries, Departments, institutions, voluntary organisations, experts, social workers, etc.
4.         The Secretary, Department of Women and Child Development apprised the Committee at its meeting held on the
16
th June, 2005 about the background for bringing the proposed legislation on protection of child rights before
Parliament.  The Secretary then touched upon the basic features of the Bill giving an idea about the composition and
appointment of the Commission, its functions, special powers, constitution of State Commissions, Children's Courts,
procedure for enquiry, presentation of its reports and other miscellaneous provisions.
5.         The Committee had invited views/suggestions from the general public through a notice published in newspapers
on various provisions of the Bill.  The Committee also had the opportunity to hear the views of a number of Voluntary
Organizations, social workers and legal persons working in areas like child welfare, protection of child rights, their
education and health, juvenile justice, child labour, etc.  These extensive deliberations and also the voluminous written
material received from all concerned, has greatly helped the Committee in formulating its views on various provisions of
this special piece of legislation, very much required for the development and protection of our future generations. 
6.         The Committee likes to place on record its appreciation for the Department for bringing out this Bill for setting up
a Commission to protect and promote interests of Children. Keeping in view vast population of children in the country,
mostly being under-privileged, setting up of such a Commission is the need of the hour. Protecting and promoting their
interest is laudable and challenging as well. The Committee after detailed discussion came to the conclusion that certain
provisions, particularly those relating to appointment and removal of the Chairperson and members of the proposed
Commission, its functions, procedure  for transaction of its business, powers relating to inquiries and children's courts
needed some amendments.  Need for adding more provisions was felt necessary to provide required autonomy as well as
powers to the proposed Commission so that it can carry out its mandate in a more credible and effective manner and it
does not appear to be a body controlled by the Government of the day.            
7.         The Committee at its meeting held on the 4
th August, 2005 took up the Bill for Clause-by-clause consideration.
The Clauses where amendments were suggested by the Committee have been discussed in the succeeding
paragraphs.        
Clause 3
8.         Sub-clause (2) (b) of clause 3 provides that six members of the Commission will be appointed by the Central
Government from amongst persons of eminence, ability, integrity, standing and experience from different fields
mentioned therein. Although, this particular Clause, Committee notes, does not prohibit the appointment of women as

165th Report of HRD Committee
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/165threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
members of the Commission, almost everybody who appeared before it, impressed upon the need for having an explicit
provision that at least two of its members have to be women.  It is a well-known fact that women have better
understanding of problems as well as needs of the children.  By ensuring women representation in the Commission, cause
of children would be served better.  The Committee also concurs with this line of thinking.  It, therefore, recommends that
out of the six members appointed to the Commission, at least two should be women.  A provision to this effect should be
inserted in the Bill.
Clause – 4
9.         The Committee notes that as per the Clause 4 of the Bill, the Chairperson and members of the Commission shall
be appointed by the Central Government.  However, appointment of the Chairperson shall be based on the
recommendation of a three member Selection Committee headed by the Minister of Human Resource Development.  The
Committee feels that this selection procedure might impinge upon the autonomy and independence required for
functioning of such a Commission.  It, therefore, is of the view that a National Commission of such a great significance
should be appointed by a higher/independent authority and certainly not by the government alone. The Committee notes
that the President of India is the appointing authority for the Chairman of the National Human Rights Commission and an
independent body having representation of high dignitaries as the Selection Committee for its members.  The Committee
strongly feels that similar provision be provided for the appointment of the Chairman and the members of the
Commission being set up for promotion of child welfare. The Committee therefore recommends that the existing Clause 4
of the Bill should be substituted by the following:-
(1)
               The Chairperson and other Members shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.

10.       Clause 5(1) provides for the term of office of the Chairman and Members of the Commission.  The Committee
notes that there is no restriction on the number of terms the Chairman or the Member of the Commission can serve.  It
feels that a specific provision in this regard is required to be made.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Chairman
and Members should not be allowed to function for more than two terms.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to
insert a provision to this effect in Clause 5(1) of the Bill.

Government, resign his office at any time.  In view of the Committee's recommendations to make President of India their
appointing authority, consequential changes in clause 5(2) should also be made.
11.2     The Committee, therefore, recommends that in sub clause (2) of Clause (5) the words “Central Government” may
be replaced by “President of India”.

wherein the vacancies might remain unfilled for a long time which may affect the functioning of the Commission
adversely.

would be required to meet at shorter intervals.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that sub clause (1) of
clause-10 may be substituted as follows:-

16.1     Sub-clause (4) of clause 10 provides that the Commission shall observe such rules of procedure for the transaction
of its business at a meeting including the quorum at such meeting, as may be prescribed by the Central Government.
16.2     On being asked about the specific reasons for not empowering the Commission to lay down its own procedure, the
Committee was informed that where a Statutory Commission was headed by a person who is/has been a Supreme
Court/High Court Judge, the regulation of the procedure is left with the Commission.  This was primarily because they
would be aware of all such rules.  In contrast, where persons from other fields are appointed as Chairpersons, rules of the
procedure are framed by the administrative Ministry in consultation with Ministry of Law.  The Committee is not
convinced by the clarifications given by the Department.  It would like to point out that this is not so in the case of the
National Commission for Women.  Its Chairperson is of similar status as envisaged for the proposed Commission, yet it
has the power to regulate its own procedure.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that sub-clause (4) of clause 10
should also provide that the Commission shall have the power to regulate its own procedure.

Clause 13
 
18.1     The Committee notices that a very crucial aspect - violation of child rights, does not occur anywhere in Clause 13
listing out functions of the Commission.  In other words, the Commission would have no power to inquire into child right
violations.  If it is so, the Committee feels, the Commission's powers shall remain highly truncated.  Besides, the Clause
15 (i) empowers the Commission to recommend initiation of proceedings in cases of violations of child rights.  The
Committee is at a loss to understand that if the Commission does not have an explicit power to go into violations of child
rights, how can it recommend such cases for action?  The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that going into violations
of child right should be expressly provided in Clause 13. 
18.2
          For this, the Committee recommends that the Clause 13 (c) and 13 (d) to be restructured as follows to make these
more harmonious and exhaustive.
(c)                examine all factors that violate and inhibit the enjoyment of rights of children and recommends appropriate
remedial measures.
(d)               look into the matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,
marginalised and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family,
children of prisoners and also children affected by terrorism, communal violence, riots, natural disasters,
domestic violence, HIV/AIDS, trafficking, mal-treatment, torture and exploitation, pornography and
prostitution and recommends appropriate remedial measures.
18.3     The Committee also recommends to add “violation and” after “deprivation” in clause 13(i) (i)
Clause 14
 
19.1     In Clause 14, the Committee notices that there is no provision to deal with tendering of false or fabricated
evidence during inquiries under clauses 13 (i) and 14 (2), empowering the Commission to refer cases to the Magistrate of
jurisdiction under section of 346 of Criminal Procedure Code, covers only cases of contempt by way of intentional refusal
to produce a document, or to take oath, or to answer questions, or to sign the statement, or intentionally insulting or
obstructing proceedings by a public servant (punishable under sections 175, 178, 179, 180 and 228 respectively of the
Indian Penal Code).  It does not, the Committee feels, empower the Commission to refer cases of "giving or fabricating
false evidence" (punishable under Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code), which can be referred to a Magistrate of
jurisdiction under section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code.  Even the term "all the powers of a civil court" used in
Clause 14 (1) does not empower the Commission to refer cases under section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code as
under sub-section (3) of this section, a public servant/Tribunal has to be specifically "declared by the relevant Act to be a
Court for the purposes of this Section".  
 
19.2     The Committee is of the considered view that without these powers, as given in Section 13 of the National Human

STATE COMMISSIONS
 
25.1     The Committee, in view of its recommendations to amend provision of the Bill relating to constitution,
appointment, removal, etc. of the National Commission recommends that the corresponding provisions pertaining to the
State Commissions should also be amended accordingly.
25.2     Chapter IV deals with the constitution of State Commissions.  The Committee observes that as per Clause 17(i), it
is not mandatory for a State Government to set up State Commission.  The Committee is somewhat worried by the
experience with quite a few State Governments not fulfilling the provision of setting up of State Human Rights
Commissions and State Commissions for Women inspite of a provision being there in the respective Acts.  The
Committee, accordingly, recommends that it should be made mandatory for every State Government/UT Administration
to set up Child Rights Commission.
 
25.3     Provisions regarding State Commissions indicate that the State Commissions will be functioning independently. 
The Committee feels that there is a need for some kind of interface and co-ordination between State Commissions and
National Commission specially in view of the experience so far with regard to State Commissions of NHRC and NWC. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that such a provision could be made in the Rules.
 
25.4     The Committee observes that there are a number of Commissions/Boards such as National Commission for
Women, National Human Rights Commission, Juvenile Justice Boards, Child Welfare Boards and Central Social Welfare
Board, all of which are directly or indirectly involved in child welfare and also in the exercise of protecting their rights. 
With the enactment of the proposed Bill and State Commissions for child rights being set up, need for effective
coordination among these bodies so as to avoid any confusion/over-lapping will be increasingly felt.   The Committee has
been informed that a National Co-ordination Group having representatives from all concerned Ministries on children
issues has been set up.  The Committee hopes that this will prove to be an effective mechanism.
 
25.5     The Committee recommends that the Bill should have a provision at appropriate place to expressly prohibit State
Commissions to take up an issue, which is under consideration of the National Commission.
Clause 25
 
26.1     The omnibus provision under Clause 25 for trial of all "offences against children" or "violation of child rights" by

'Children's Courts' in Committee's view, would be difficult to implement and could lead to complications/conflicts in view
of the following factors:
(i)                  While offences committed against children or crimes in which children are the victims are considered as
'offences against children', there is no separate classification of such offences under the IPC and Criminal
procedure Code, which could be earmarked for trial by such courts. 
 
(ii)                In cases where the victims comprise both children as well as adults, there cannot be separate trials in two
different courts of the same offender(s) for the same offence.
 
(iii)   Offences in which the offenders are also juveniles are triable by Juvenile Justice Board under the Juvenile Justice
(Care and Protection) Act, 2000, and cannot be tried by Children's Courts under this Bill.
 
(iv)              All 'violations of child rights' may not amount to punishable offences triable by such courts.
 
26.2     In the light of the above observations the Committee feels that suitable amendments/additions should be made in
the Clause 25 with a view to ensure speedy trial of cases relating to Children.

27.       The Committee observes that human rights and child rights are integrated and inter related.  It would only be
appropriate if the two Commissions have some interface in their working at the higher levels.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Chairperson of the National Commission may be deemed to a Member of the National Human
Rights Commission.  The Department may take this up with the Ministry concerned for bringing an amendment to this
effect in the NHRC Act.

CHAPTER-II
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF GOVERNMENTS’ REPLY
 
V         ISSUES FOR GENDER BUDGETING
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
4.1       The Committee is of the opinion that in view of integration of gender equality with sustainable development,
need and importance of gender budgeting can hardly be over emphasized.  The aim of gender budgeting is to
generate/capture the gender-based data/information, which will be relevant  input for assessing the gender specific
impact of budgetary allocations.  The Committee found that currently gender segregated macro-economic data were not
available in India.  In the absence of such data from different sectors of our economy, the Committee feels it will be
difficult to analyse the budgetary allocations on the basis of gender.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
process of gender budgeting should necessarily contain not only the segregation of gender based data but also aspects
like quantification of contribution of women in the economy; impact of Government budget on women; and policy
alternatives for evolving a gender sensitive social order.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
4.1       Recognizing the need to widen the ambit of gender budgeting, the Department held a consultation on 8
December 2004, with experts and representatives of various Government organizations and para-statal bodies to arrive
at a consensus on the framework of gender budgeting.  The meeting was chaired by Secretary (WCD) and was attended
by Advisor, Planning Commission, Joint Secretary (Budget), Member, NCW, representatives of UNIFEM and UNDP
and a few social experts.  The Department has adopted the following slogan as a mission statement for gender budgeting
–
 
            ‘Budgeting for Gender Equity’
 
The broad-framework recommended for gender budget analysis is as follows
 
Broad framework of activities
Quantification of allocation of resources for women in the Union, States and Local Administration budgets
and expenditure thereof.
q       Refining and standardizing methodology and development of tools.

q       Trend Analysis
q       Analysis of change in pattern, shift in priorities in allocation across clusters of services etc
q       Variations in allocation of resources and actual expenditure
q       Adherence to physical targets
 
Gender Audit of policies of the Government- monetary, fiscal, trade etc. at the Centre and State levels
q       Research and micro studies to guide macro policies like credit policy, taxes etc
q       Identification of gender impact of policies/interventions viewed as gender neutral
q       Micro studies to identify need for affirmative action in favour of women towards correcting gender imbalances
 
Impact assessment of various schemes in the Union and State budgets
q       Micro studies on incidence of benefits
q       Analysis of cost of delivery of services
 
Analyzing programmes, strategies, interventions and policy initiatives from the perspective of their impact
on status of women as reflected in important Macro Indicators like literacy, MMR, participation in work
force
q       E.g.- analysis of substance and content of various interventions directed at health of women and correlate the same
with indicator like MMR to establish need for corrective action in formulation of scheme/ approach.
 
Institutionalizing the generation and collection of gender dis-aggregated data
q       Developing MIS for feed back from implementing agencies
q       Inclusion of new parameters in data collection in Census and surveys by NSO, CSO etc
 
Consultations and Capacity building
q       Collation of research and exchange of best practices
q       Developing methodologies and tools for dissemination
q       Forums and Partnerships amongst experts and stakeholders.
 
Review of decision making processes to establish gender equity in participation-  review of extant
participation of women in decision making processes and to establish processes and models aimed at gender
equity in decision making and greater participation of women.
 
Formulation and reflection of satellite accountsto capture the contribution of women to the economy by
way of their activities in areas that go unreported like care economy, unpaid work in rearing domestic
animals etc.
 
It may be seen that various concerns expressed by the   Committee are part of the framework. As a coordinating
Department in Gender matters, we would be pursuing the gender budgeting mandate with all Departments.         This
framework has been communicated to all Ministries of Government of India to guide their further actions in terms of
allocation of resources and review of policy.
 
V         ROLE OF DEPARTMENT OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
5.3       After looking at these efforts made by the Department, the Committee notes that so far, this exercise had
remained confined mainly to holding Seminars/Workshops since November 1998.  The Committee is of the opinion that
the exercise of gender budgeting was not being carried out with the seriousness that it deserved.  The Committee feels
that the exercises undertaken by the Department so far, were hardly enough to sensitize the other Ministries and
Departments of the Government of India for undertaking this important activity.  Perhaps, the idea of making the
Department of Women & Child Development as a nodal agency for undertaking this exercise was to do the ground
exercise and evolve methodologies, etc. to be later on adopted by other Ministries/Departments for gender budgeting in
an organized and comprehensive manner.  The Committee is constrained to say that unfortunately this has not happened

166th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/166threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
and we have not been able to evolve till today the required tools, methodologies and institutional mechanisms for
segregating gender based data, leave alone the quantification of contribution of women in the economy and the impact
of budgetary allocations on the women in our society.  Unless it is done, the Committee firmly believes, the goal of the
gender budgeting shall remain elusive.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
5.3       The Department of Women and Child Development had commissioned the National Institute of Public Finance
and Policy to undertake a study on gender related economic policy issues to cover: Parameters to identify status of
women; Quantification of contribution of women; Assessing impact of Government Budget on women; Role women
can play in improving institutional framework for delivery of public services.
 
            Based on the interim report of the NIPFP, (January 2001), for the first time, the Economic Survey 2000-01
highlighted issues like, Gender Inequality and Status of Women.  Thus gender equality and empowerment of women
have been recognized as economic goals.  It is continued as regular feature every year.
 
            The second interim report of the NIPFP (August 2001), analysed the Union Budget 2001-02 from a gender
perspective.
 
            The model for analyzing the Union Budget developed by the NIPFP was carried forward by the Department to
analyse the Union Budget 2002-03 and 2003-04.  In 2002-03 a research study was also commissioned to undertake
gender analysis of all State budgets.  The report has since been received and results of preliminary analysis are reflected
in the annual report of 2004-05.
 
The Department of Women and Child Development is actively participating in the inter departmental committee
constituted by the Ministry of Finance for evolving the methodology for analysis of public expenditure from a gender
perspective.  Secretary (WCD) attended the first inter-Departmental Meeting chaired by Secretary, Expenditure on 7
December 2004. Action is thus on to develop a model for gender analysis of public expenditure
 
VI        GENDER BUDGETING IN OTHER MINISTRIES/DEPARTMENTS
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
6.4       The Committee is of the opinion that gender based analysis of allocations should be done for the entire Budget
of the Government.  This exercise, therefore, will have to be taken up by all the Ministries/Departments of the
Government of India, not only by those identified for this purpose so far.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the remaining ones should also be sensitized to infuse gender aspects into their allocations/expenditure without further
delay.  This is necessary to have holistic idea about gender-based allocations of the entire Budget of the Government of
India.  The Department of Women and Child Development being a nodal agency should assume greater responsibilities
for undertaking this exercise of the gender budgeting by all the Ministries/Departments without further delay.
 
6.5       The Committee notes that the objective of gender budgeting is there, the Ministries/Departments are identified,
but the results are not forthcoming in absence of any guidelines for this purpose.  The Committee fails to understand the
Department’s limitations in this regard.  The Committee recommends to have specific guidelines laid down regarding
gender budgeting to be followed by all the Ministries/Departments.  This would still be quite possible on the basis of
experiences/feedback received on the problems being faced in implementation of gender budgeting.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
6.4 & 6.5         The issue of gender based analysis of allocation being undertaken for the entire budget has been
addressed in the deliberations of the inter-departmental committee set up by the Ministry of Finance.  The Department
of Women and Child Development is an active integral part of this committee and   pressed for setting up of gender
budget cells in all Ministries and Departments so that there is a point of focus for coordinating gender friendly initiatives
for the Department of Women and Child Development.  Instructions have so far been issued for only 18 Ministries so

3.5       In the context of India, where the gender bias is inherent in a male-dominated society, Gender Budgeting
becomes all the more relevant.  The Committee observes that the trends in sex ratio and other socio-economic indicators
clearly show, how the bias is getting accentuated in many parts of the country.  Over the years, during the course of
examination of various women and girl child related programmes/schemes, one factor which has been constantly
drawing the attention of the Committee is that in spite of well-conceived programmes and the funds allocated, there has
been no noticeable improvement in the status of women/girls.   Recently released State specific sex ratio figures of
Census 2001, do not leave any doubt in this regard.  The Committee is of the view that it is high time that the Budget of
the Government provides a clear indication of how much is earmarked specifically for the benefit of women so as to
ensure effective implementation of women/girl related programmes.  Department of Women & Child Development is
not only the nodal agency for such programmes but also the nodal Department assigned with carrying out the task of
Gender Budgeting, the Committee accordingly decided to make a study on work done so far in this emerging area.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.5       The Department of Women and Child Development has been undertaking the role of a coordinating  
Department through monitoring of 27 beneficiary oriented schemes since 1985. The exercise of quantifying resources
earmarked for women was entrusted to the National institute  of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP) and they developed
a model for gender analysis of the Union Budget, beginning with the Union Budget for 2001-2002. This model has  
been adopted by the Department to quantify allocation for women in the Union Budget for subsequent years.  
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the model for gender based analysis of the Union Budget developed by
NIPFP in 2001-2002, needs to be refined with a view to making it more precise and wider in scope. This model is not
able to provide adequate insight in the case of mainstream budgets. The Committee, therefore, recommends that steps be
taken to examine the same and a methodology evolved on this aspect at the earliest.

September 27, 2005                                                                                                                                            Chairman,

REPORT
The National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions (Amendment) Bill, 2005 seeks to amend the National
Commission for Minority Educational Institutions Act, 2004, which provided to set up a Commission to advise the
Central Government or any State Government on any question relating to the education of minorities that may be
referred to it; to look into specific complaints regarding deprivation or violation of rights of minorities to establish and
administer educational institutions; to decide on any dispute relating to affiliation to a Scheduled University; and to
report its findings to the Central Government for its implementation. The said Act also provided right to a Minority
Educational Institution (MEI) to seek affiliation to any of six Universities listed in its schedule. The Commission was
also given power to determine disputes regarding affiliation between Minority Educational Institutions and the
Universities.
2.         The Committee was informed that based on the experience of the functioning of the Commission, it was felt that
by limiting the scope of affiliation only to six Universities given in the Schedule to the Act, the applicability of the Act
had been severely restricted. The Commission as well as the Government received several representations and
suggestions for making the Commission more effective in deciding on matters of deprivation or violation of the
educational rights of the minorities guaranteed under Article 30 of the Constitution. The majority of the representations
received by the Commission related to the problems faced by minority communities in obtaining ‘No Objection
Certificate’ (NOC) for establishing an Educational Institution and also in obtaining the status of a Minority Institution.
3.         The Amending Bill, accordingly, seeks to empower the Commission to be more effective and proactive in
protecting the educational rights of minorities in respect of seeking affiliation to universities; seeking NOC for setting
up MEIs; and in obtaining minority status without any harassment.
4.         The salient features of the Bill are as follows:-
It provides for the right to establish a Minority Educational Institution and also provides that wherever ‘No Objection
Certificate’ for establishing a Minority Educational Institution is either not granted within a period of sixty days or
where a decision in this regard is not communicated within such period, the Minority Educational Institution would
proceed with the establishment of the institution as if the No Objection Certificate has been granted to it.
It provides for the right of Minority Educational Institutions to seek affiliation to any University of their choice subject
to the Acts, Statutes, Ordinances, Rules and Regulations of the concerned University. It proposes to do away with the
Schedule.
It also proposes to give appellate jurisdiction to the Commission in the matters of refusal to grant ‘No Objection
Certificate’ for establishing a Minority Educational Institution.
It enables the National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions to enquire into and investigate complaints
regarding deprivation or violation of rights of minorities to establish and administer Educational Institutions of their
choice and, also to decide on disputes relating to affiliation of Minority Educational Institutions to a University.
It also enables the Commission to decide on all questions relating to the status of any institution as a Minority
Educational Institution.
It empowers the Commission to cancel recognition as a Minority Educational Institution, where it is found by the
Commission that the purpose or character on which a Minority Educational Institution status was granted and also in
admitting students belonging to the minority community as per rules and prescribed percentage, has failed.
It provides that every proceeding before the Commission shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding and, the orders
made by the Commission shall be executable by it as a decree of a civil court.
It empowers the Commission to utilize the services of any officer of the Central Government or any State Government,
with the concurrence of such Government, for the purpose of conducting investigation pertaining to complaints received
by the Commission.
It bars the jurisdiction of Courts (except the Supreme Court and the High Courts) to entertain any suit, application or
other proceedings in respect of orders made by the Commission.
5.         The Committee, heard the Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education and took up `clause-by-
clause’ consideration of the Bill. It suggested the following amendments/additions to various clauses of the Bill.

Clause 1
6.1       The Committee notes that the present Bill does not contain the commencement clause.
6.2       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the date of commencement of the Amendment Bill may be
included in the corpus of the Bill.
Clause 3
7.1       The Committee notes that clause 3 of the Bill seeks to substitute section 10 in chapter III of the principal Act
with new clauses 10 and 10 A. Under the proposed clause 10, any person desiring to establish a Minority Educational
Institution may apply for a ‘No Objection Certificate’ from the competent authority, who shall decide every application
expeditiously.  In order to prevent delays on the part of the competent authority in granting the required NOC, a
provision in clause 10(3) is being made enabling the applicant to proceed with establishing an institution under the
relevant law, if the competent authority does not grant the certificate or fails to communicate the refusal, to the
applicant. It would then be deemed, as if the NOC has been granted.
7.2       The Committee feels that the deeming provision contained in clause 10(3) regarding the grant of NOC
after a period of 60 days, would allow enough scope for its frequent misuse. Chances of delaying the
communication from the office of the competent authority to the applicant either in his office or in transit cannot
be ruled out. The Committee is concerned about the possibility of a situation where communication about a
rejected application is so delayed and the applicant goes ahead with establishing an MEI after 60 days.
Therefore, adequate safeguards against possible abuses of this provision, need to be provided in the Bill itself.
One such measure, the Committee recommends, could be to extend the period of 60 days to 90 days.
7.3       The Committee also recommends that the person making an application for NOC may approach the competent
authority after a period of 60 days of submitting the application, to know about the status of his application.  A provision
for this should be made in the Bill.
7.4       The Committee notes that Section 10A of clause 3 provides that a Minority Educational Institution may seek
affiliation to any affiliating University of its choice, thereby removing the limitation for seeking affiliation to only a
Scheduled University. The applicant would be expected to seek affiliation in terms of the procedures prescribed by the
relevant Statutes, Ordinances or rules of the University.
7.5       The Committee has a strong apprehension about allowing MEIs to seek affiliation to a university of their choice,
irrespective of distance or geographical contiguity which is an important consideration for the convenience of both, the
universities as well as MEIs.  Secondly, the Committee feels that the good and reputed universities may face  problems
because all the MEIs would generally prefer to be affiliated to the best ones.  Although this choice of MEIs, the
Committee notes, would be limited by the provisions in the Acts, Statutes/rules of the universities, the Committee
neverthless emphasizes that some kind of restriction regarding geographical contiguity or State boundary must be
provided in the Bill itself.
Clause 4
8.1       Clause 4 proposes to amend Section 11 of the principal Act. Clause 4(c)  of the proposed amendment
empowers the Commission to intervene in any judicial proceedings, with the leave of the Court, in matters
involving deprivation of educational rights of minorities.
8.2       With regard to the question of the overall authority of the Commission to intervene in the Court, the Secretary,
Department of Secondary and Higher Education submitted before the Committee that it is an area in which a lot of
frivolous litigations come in and there are a lot of things which come in to hurt the interests of Minority Institutions. In
such a case, the Government, felt that the Commission should have some authority to intervene. It is therefore, an
enabling provision.
8.3       The Committee, as regards clause 4 (c ), feels that the power of the Commission to intervene in Court
cases involving deprivation of minority educational  rights  before a Court, may push the whole thing under
litigation.    If suo motu, the Court calls the Commission, there is no problem. Otherwise, the Committee, feels
that the Commission would become a frontrunner in a variety of considerations. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the intervention of the Commission in Court proceeding  might be restricted to those cases only
where the Courts demand it.
Clause 6
9.1       Under clause six new sections (12A to 12F) are proposed to be inserted in Section 12 of the Principal Act. In
order to prevent the misuse of minority status by institutions, it is being provided under section 12C that the
Commission shall cancel recognition as a Minority Educational Institution, in case the Commission finds that the
purpose or character for which an Educational Institution was granted a minority status has been amended or the
institution has failed in admitting students belonging to the minority community as per rules and prescribed percentage

167th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/167threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:38]
governing admissions during any academic year.
9.2       The Committee recommends that on cancellation of the Minority Status of the institution, the provisions of this
Act shall cease to apply to such institution.
9.3 The Committee feels that the Bill must provide adequate safeguards for preventing the misuse of the `Minority
Status’ by an institution.
10.       The Committee adopts the remaining clauses of the Bill without any amendments.
11.       The enacting formula and the title are adopted with consequential changes.
12.       The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendment /additions suggested
by it. 
13.       The Committee would like the Department to submit a note with reasons on the recommendations/suggestions
made by the Committee, which could not be incorporated in the Bill.

NOTE OF DISSENT
                                                                                                                                      RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD
                                                                                                                                                   Senior Advocate
                                                                                                                                             M.P., RAJYA SABHA
                                                                       
NOTE OF DISSENT
ON THE NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR MINORITY EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS (AMENDMENT)
BILL 2005
The above Bill seeks to comprehensively amend the “National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions Act
2005 (Act 2 of 2005)”. It is indeed surprising that the Act, which come into force only on 7
th of January 2005 is sought
to be amended by the Bill, which was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 23rd of August 2005. What were the compelling
circumstances, which required such a comprehensive amendment only after seven month, still remains unclear?
All of us agree with the proposition that minorities must be given opportunity to establish institution of their choice but
there is no empirical evidence available that the original Act, which only came into force on 7th of January 2005, was
posing so much difficulty in the fulfillment of the said objective that required such far reaching change. Obviously it can
not be because seven month is too short a period to examine the results of the working of any particular legislation.
Though, one acknowledges the right of the executive to bring the Bill but the hurried manner in which such far reaching
amendments are being introduced raises disturbing questions.
Of particular concern is the complete denial of any role of the State Government in the amendment Bill. Under the
original Act 2 of 2005 under Section 10 (ii) it was the obligatory on the part of the schedule University to consult the
Government of the State concerned and consider its view before granting affiliation. This provision has been given a
complete go by the amended Bill besides impinging upon the federal character of the Constitution. Besides the power of
the States it raises serious question of security. Only the State Government through its various organizations has the
capacity to discover the source of funding and the background of the people who have promoted the institutions in
question. The University granting affiliation does not have the infrastructure or the ability to inquire into these
circumstances.
It is again reiterated that minority should be encouraged to pursue their right to establish and administer their own
institutions. However, the troubled times in which we all live in India, issues of security concerned can not be brushed
aside altogether. Terrorist violence in most of the cases being sponsored by forces from across the border has become
the order of the day. Even the national capital is not spared. Terrorists are using different fronts as we see day after day.
Therefore, some suitable provision need be there to ensure that any particular institutions seeking protection and
affiliation under the Act may not become a front of some terrorist operations i.e. it’s sponsored and financers have links
with the terrorist network. Obviously, the State Government only has the ability and capacity to know these things.
Therefore, it is eminently desirable and in abiding public and national interest the view of the State Government must be
sought as originally enshrined in the main Act 2 of 2005. I have a very serious view on this issue, which I had
highlighted during the course of meeting of H.R.D. Standing Committee, hence this note of dissent.
It is equally important that geographical contiguity of the University with the affiliating minority institutions must be
duly kept in mind.
                                                                                                                                Sd/-(Ravi Shankar Prasad)

Para 2.10
            The Committee observes that during the first three years of the Tenth Plan although level of allocated funds
remained same, the Department failed to utilize them fully.  Plan allocation for 2005-06 shows an increase of Rs. 486.00
crores when compared with 2004-05 allocations.  The Department should take all the required steps for optimum and
judicious utilization of funds allocated for 2005-06.  The Department should desist from undertaking last minute spending. 
Expenditure should be more or less evenly in all the quarters of the year.
 
ACTION TAKEN:
The comments of the Parliamentary Standing Committee have been noted for compliance.  All efforts will be made
to ensure even spread of expenditure during 2005-06.
 
IV        NATIONAL COUNCIL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH & TRAINING
 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
Para 4.2
The Committee notes that despite various new initiatives proposed by NCERT to carry out in the year 2005-06,
allocation to it has been kept the same as that of last year.  This points to the fact that programmes and initiatives have been
envisaged without adequate financial backing.  The Committee, therefore, apprehends that the proposed new initiatives as
well as its on going programmes might suffer due to want of funds in the year 2005-06.  Therefore, more funds may be
given for NCERT at RE stage.
 
ACTION TAKEN:

Para 18.1       
The Scheme of Community Polytechnics was started during the year 1978-79 as a Direct Central Assistance
Scheme of the Government of India  with the aim of harnessing  the scientific/technical knowledge available with
Polytechnics to secure Community/Rural Development.  The region-wise distribution of Community Polytechnic is given

The allocation in BE 2004-2005 for Community Polytechnics was Rs. 29.23 crores, which was increased to Rs.

allocation has been only Rs.11.05 crores as on 4.3.2005 which is a mere 34.84 per cent of the allocation.   The Committee
would like the Department to see that the funds  for 2005-06 are utilized properly and judiciously for such an important
scheme.
 
Para 18.3
           
The Committee observes that the Scheme of Community Polytechnics although started in 1978-79 has failed to
make the desired impact so far.  During the Ninth Plan against a target of 14 lakh persons, only 11 lakh persons could be
trained in various non-formal job-oriented skills.  Funds allocated also remained underutilized.  Expenditure of only Rs.
97.87 crore could be made against an allocation of Rs. 297.26 crores.  During the first three years of Tenth Plan also, funds
remained underutilized.  The Committee notes that in 2002-03, allocation of Rs. 65.00 crore had to be reduced to Rs. 37
crores and against that reduced allocation of unspent balances lying with Community Polytechnics  was adjusted.  The
other reason for underutilization is prolonged process of revision of the Scheme.  During 2002-03 and 2003-04 EFC
proposal could not be finalized.  It was only in 2004-05 that  EFC was finalized at the Department level. Comments from
some Ministries, including Planning Commission are awaited.  The Committee is constrained to observe that the meeting
of EFC could not be held by the end of March 2005.  The Committee can only hope that the restructured Scheme can be
implemented perhaps in the end of Tenth Plan, i.e. 2006-07.
 
Para 18.4
           
The Committee feels that the regional distribution of Community Polytechnics is uneven.  Particularly, eastern
region has only 97 Community Polytechnics.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Department should try to open
more Community Polytechnics in eastern region which is a backward area having the highest concentration of rural
population.   The imparting of technical skills will help ameliorate the pitiable conditions prevailing there.  The Committee
feels that the underutilization of funds must have affected the training programmes, thereby defeating the very objective of
the Scheme.

ACTION TAKEN (18.1 to 18.4):
            Against a BE of Rs 29.23 crores in 2004-05, the amount finally released to Community Polytechnics as on
31.03.2005 was Rs.20.79 crores. The savings with reference to BE are a result of adjustment of Unspent Adjustment lying
with some Community Polytechnics and delay in finalization of EFC for restructuring the scheme.  The EFC envisaged
phased expansion of the Scheme, including selection of 20 new Community Polytechnics in 2004-05, involving a total
outlay of Rs. 4.90 crores.
 
In an attempt to further improve the funds utilization, a series of State-level review meetings / workshops have been
organized at various locations in the country, in the months of April and May 2005, by the Regional Resource Institutions
i.e. National Institute of Technical Teachers Training & Research (NITTTRs). These Meetings were attended by the
Principals of the Community Polytechnics and representatives of the State Directorates of Technical, which administer the
Polytechnics. The Principals have been sensitized to the need to further improve the utilization of funds.
 
            As noted by the Committee, the EFC meeting could not be held in the last financial year because comments from
the appraisal Ministries including Planning Commission had not been received. Pursuant to the circulation of the EFC, the
Project Appraisal and Monitoring Division in Planning Commission undertook a detailed appraisal of the Scheme before
furnishing their comments in the month of   May, 2005. Planning Commission have, based on their appraisal of the
Scheme, suggested some modifications to the EFC proposal, which are being examined by the Ministry. The Department is
making a conscientious effort to speed up the process of obtaining EFC approval for the revised Scheme.
 
As regards the physical progress, against around 11 lakh persons trained during the 5 years of the IX Plan period,
more than 6 Lakh persons have already availed of the non-formal training programmes offered by the Community
Polytechnics in various job-oriented skills, in the first two years of the 10th Plan. It is expected that the overall performance
during the 10th Plan will continue to reflect this trend of improvement.
 
            Scheme of Community Polytechnics  is implemented only through AICTE approved Diploma Level Institutions
(Polytechnics) which are under the Administrative Control of State Governments. As there are less number of polytechnic
level institutions in the Eastern Region compared to other regions, the number of Community Polytechnics are also less. As
per the information received from the State Directorates of Technical Education, most of the Govt./Govt. Aided
Polytechnics of the States of Eastern Region have been covered under the Scheme.
           
The issue of expanding the Scheme's coverage in the Eastern Region was also raised by the Department related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on HRD previously, in it's 145
th Report. Pursuant to the Committee's observation, the
Department had engaged in an exercise to consult the concerned State Governments as well as AICTE on this issue and a
meeting was also organised by AICTE with representatives of State Directorates of Technical Education of the concerned
States.  The State Government representatives observed that increasing the number of Polytechnics in the Region may not
be possible. However all of them were of the view that more extension centers may be allowed in the region under existing
Community Polytechnics to cover a larger area.
 
            Keeping in mind the views of the State Governments, the Ministry has included a proposal in the draft EFC for
restructuring the Scheme, under which all Community Polytechnics of the NE Region and J & K will be allowed to operate
15 Extension Centres (as compared to 5 at present). The annual recurring grant for the Community Polytechnics of NE
Region are also proposed to be enhanced to meet the expenditure on the additional Extension Centres. It is expected that
the above proposal when implemented will ensure adequate coverage of the rural population in the NE Region, under the
Scheme of Community Polytechnics, in a cost effective manner.

CCEA after formation of  new Government, after obtaining approval of the new Minister-in-Charge and fresh inter-
Ministerial Consultations.  After the new Government was formed, the fresh approval of new HRD Minister was obtained
and inter-Ministerial Consultations were held again.
 
                        Finally, the Cabinet approved the ICT @ Schools Scheme on 15th December, 2004. Immediately after the
approval of the Cabinet, the ICT @ Schools Scheme was circulated to all the States/UTs with the request to submit their
Computer Education Plans as per the norms of the ICT @ Schools Scheme. It was decided that to begin with, financial
assistance would be released to the States/UT/Organizations on the basis of the actual expenditure incurred by them on the
revised CLASS Scheme. So far, for the currently year, we have received Computer Education Plans from 16 States and this
Department is hopeful that it will fully utilize the entire budget of Rs. 50.00 crores allocated for the Scheme during 2005-
06.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee appreciates that the Department’s will to fully utilize the budget of Rs. 50.00 crores allocated for
the ICT in Schools Scheme.  However, the Committee is surprised to note that it took almost two years to send a Cabinet
Note for approval of the ICT in Schools Scheme to CCEA after getting approval from the HRD Minister and holding inter-
Ministerial consultations. The Committee is happy to see that later on the procedure was expedited in few months. The
Committee hopes that the Department will continue to be proactive and efficient in discharging its duties.

Para  11.7      
Even though the Department has been requesting the District Magistrate to carry out the inspection of the hostels,
in most of the cases it has been found that inspection has been done by some lower level officials of the State Government. 
The Committee recommends that the State Governments may be directed to depute a senior officer of Education

ACTION TAKEN:
 
             The observations of the Committee have been noted.  In the Scheme, it has been stipulated that the State
Governments have to forward the applications of NGOs for consideration by the Government of India.  However, this is
either not done or takes a very long time.  In several individual cases, Government has written directly to District
Magistrates and sought replies.  However, State Government endorsements are normally given very routinely.  Instructions
to State Governments are being issued again.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee is not happy with the reply of the Department that the Ministry is issuing the reminder/instructions
to the State Governments.  The Committee is aware of the workload of the District Magistrates and at times they may not
be able to personally inspect the hostels.  It is in this backdrop that the Committee recommended that if the District
Magistrates were not available, some other Officer may be authorized to inspect the hostels on his behalf.  The Committee,
therefore, reiterates that a Senior Officer may be authorized for carrying out the required inspections.  This issue can be
discussed and sorted out at the higher level at the earliest.
 
XIII     CENTRAL BOARD OF SECONDARY EDUCATION (CBSE)
 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
 
Para No.13.3
The Committee is of the view that besides examination stress, there are various other contributory factors such as
parental pressure, increasing competition, fast changing social and economic  conditions, etc. which cause depression in
students.  The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the CBSE and hopes that these measures would result in
giving a better environment to students.  The Committee feels that the current practice of holding Board exams for
Secondary and Senior Secondary students at schools other than their own, also generates a kind of fear psychosis amongst
them.   The Committee is of the view that in order to avoid this, holding board examinations in their own schools, with
supervisors/invigilators from different schools, may also be considered.
 
ACTION TAKEN:    
            The CBSE has taken various measures to reduce the fear about examinations which includes restructuring of question
papers thus reducing the number of questions and also to provide options and internal choices.     It has considerably reduced
the panic situation because there is an alternative option to which students can respond.  The Board always promotes quality
education which also includes conducting examination in a very professional manner.  It also ensures that there is no unfair
practices and cheating in the examinations.
 
As per the norm for fixation of examination centre, an examination centre is created subject to the availability of the
bank/treasury facilities for the safe custody of question papers and also the availability of appropriate number of rooms with
ventilation, fan, light, furniture, access to school and overall safety to ensure fair and smooth conduct of examination.
 
In the case of CBSE, the schools are mostly  situated in urban areas and the students are not required to travel long
distances to reach the examination centre.  In order to reduce fear psychosis and feeling of being in an unknown school, the
CBSE has also made it mandatory to depute teachers at the examination centre from the school whose students are appearing
at the examination centre. 
 
In places having single CBSE school, a self-centre is created in that school itself and the students are allowed to take
up the examination in their own school.  In the case of a self-centre, the Centre Superintendent is appointed from outside the
Centre and Supervisory staff is appointed from among those who are not the employees of the same school.
